Modern.brandNameRationale: Two words. Game Loop is the design term for the cycle that makes a game work: input, feedback, reward, repeat. The brand sits on the technical truth of what makes games engaging, said in the customer's own language.
Modern.industrySummary: Indie and mid-size game studios are competing with the biggest entertainment companies in the world. Brand is doing more work than ever. Studios that look like product companies on day one are getting acquired, funded, and noticed.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Annapurna Interactive (annapurnainteractive.com) holds the design-led studio benchmark. Devolver Digital (devolverdigital.com) owns the irreverent indie publisher position. Panic (panic.com) is the closest peer in clean, considered branding. We borrow Panic's restraint with a sharper modern edge.
Modern.positioningStatement: A modern game studio that ships small games well.

targetAudience.primary: Players in their late 20s through 40s. Owns a Steam library they don't have time to play. Reads RPS or Polygon. Picks games based on the studio name. Buys before sale price.

dos: Show the game, not the trailer

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. GAME LOOP in a custom geometric sans, all caps, two words on one line. The two O's in LOOP set tightly to suggest a cycle. A small standalone double-O mark for app icons, social profiles, and Steam capsule corners.

colorPalette.name: Editor Black
colorPalette.meaning: Dark theme background, the native habitat.

typography.primary: Inter for the marketing site and product
typography.secondary: JetBrains Mono for changelog and credits
typography.rationale: Inter for marketing pages. A real coding font for the changelog, credits, and developer notes. One technical, one approachable.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No early access for unfinished games. No premium currencies. No paid mod marketplaces. No promoted Steam reviews.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A studio site that shows the games and the team, in that order. A monthly devlog. Steam pages with capsule art that all share a system. No social media presence beyond a single Bluesky account run by the studio account.

Modern.brandDescription: A modern game studio that ships small games well.
Modern.mission: To build a modern game studio that ships small games well.
Modern.vision: Studios that look like product companies on day one are getting acquired, funded, and noticed.

Modern — we build for the customer reading this on a phone.
Direct — we say what we mean without softening it.
Confident — we stand behind the work, not the marketing.

GAME LOOP delivers by:
• Show the game, not the trailer

• Skip the hype copy

Luxury.brandNameRationale: The Salon evokes the 18th century intellectual gathering, where ideas were exchanged in someone's drawing room. We named the studio after that tradition, not the gaming one. Games are a medium for thinking, the brand says.
Luxury.story: The Salon began with a small group of designers and writers who wanted to make games the way intellectuals once gathered. Few people, long conversations, ideas treated with weight. The studio has stayed small on purpose. Each game takes years.
Luxury.industrySummary: Premium gaming has been dominated by big productions and bigger marketing. There's a parallel market for short, considered, almost literary games. Two-hour experiences that ship rarely and stay in collections. We belong in that small category.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Annapurna Interactive (annapurnainteractive.com) sits in the closest tier. Cardboard Computer (cardboardcomputer.com), creators of Kentucky Route Zero, is the spiritual peer. Tale of Tales (tale-of-tales.com), before they closed, did this in a previous era. We pick up that thread.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A studio for games that take less than three hours and stay with you for years.

targetAudience.primary: Players in their 30s and 40s. Reads literary fiction. Owns one good set of headphones and one tablet. Buys two games a year. Talks about them at dinner.

dos: Speak as a designer, not a publisher
Reference literature and film where it fits
Send a paper note to players who buy at full price

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small drawn-curtain hallmark, two thin vertical strokes with a slight pleat, used on the launcher splash, the printed art book, and the wax seal on the limited physical editions.

typography.rationale: A high contrast serif sets the literary register. A modern grotesk handles the few functional UI surfaces.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No live-service games. No in-game purchases. No early access. No franchise sequels. No celebrity voice casts.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Two words. Open Play is the sports term for unstructured time on the field. The brand puts the most basic version of play in the brand position. Plain. Inviting. No genre, no platform, no IP. Just the action.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most game studios have elaborate names, mascots, and brand worlds. There's an opening for one that strips it all back. One word. One mark. Many games.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most studios fail this purity test. The closest in spirit is Hempuli (hempuli.com), the solo studio behind Baba Is You, and certain Japanese studio practices like Toby Fox's solo output.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A studio that makes games. That's the whole brand.

targetAudience.primary: Players who don't need a brand world. They buy the game, not the studio. They will play anything that's good and ignore anything that isn't.

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. OPEN PLAY in a single weight grotesk, wide kerned, all caps, two words on one line. No icon. The Steam page header is the wordmark above the game name. The game name is always larger than the studio name.

typography.rationale: One face. The studio name appears once, in the splash, then gets out of the way.

customSections.title: Not this
customSections.body: No mascot. No studio T-shirts. No discord server. No development livestreams. No early access.

Minimal.brandDescription: A studio that makes games. That's the whole brand.
Minimal.mission: To build a studio that makes games. That's the whole brand.
coreValues: Plain — plain language survives every translation.
Honest — including when the answer is one we'd rather not give.
Direct — we say what we mean without softening it.
Patient — we play long games, not loud ones.
Minimal.scope:
OPEN PLAY delivers by:
• Show the game
• Show the price
• Show the platform

Corporate.tagline: A portfolio approach to interactive entertainment.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Tessera is the word for a single tile in a mosaic. The whole picture is made of pieces. The name signals a holding company that builds the larger picture out of smaller studios. Gaming Group closes it formally.
Corporate.industrySummary: Gaming has matured into a multi-hundred-billion-dollar industry. Behind the visible studios sit holding companies that consolidate, license, fund, and operate. Most of them lean either toward pure financial engineering (Embracer) or toward strict creative leadership (Take-Two). The opening is a structured, mid-size group with real operating discipline.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Embracer Group (embracer.com) is the consolidation peer. Take-Two Interactive (take2games.com) holds the operationally-disciplined side. Tencent (tencent.com) is the strategic peer at scale. We sit smaller than any of them, focused on the contemporary indie-to-mid-size tier.
Corporate.positioningStatement: A holding company building a portfolio of contemporary game studios.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Independent studios need scale partners. Investors need a disciplined operator. We sit in the middle, professionalizing what was previously fragmented across many smaller players.

targetAudience.primary: Studio founders considering acquisition, institutional investors evaluating gaming exposure, and licensing partners across publishing, distribution, and IP.
motivations: Long-term commitment to the studios' creative independence

dos: Speak to the founder and the investor
donts: Run a content strategy aimed at players

messagingPillars.name: A portfolio approach

messagingPillars.name: Long-term capital
messagingPillars.description: We hold studios for decades, not quarters. Founders retain creative authority for the life of the studio.

messagingPillars.name: Operational discipline
messagingPillars.description: Shared finance, legal, publishing, and platform relations. The studios make games. We handle the rest.

Corporate.logoDirection: A wordmark with a small geometric mark to the left. The mark is a single tessellated shape, four quadrilaterals fitted together like a mosaic tile. Reads cleanly on a quarterly investor deck, a name badge, and a press release header.

typography.primary: Inter for the website and digital
typography.secondary: Source Serif Pro for printed annual reports
typography.rationale: Inter scales clean across digital and B2B portals. The serif handles printed investor materials and annual reports.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No direct-to-player marketing. No retail games sold under the parent brand. No e-sports investments. No celebrity-streamer partnerships. The holding company is not a brand for players.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words. Already in the gaming customer's vocabulary. Hard Mode is the difficulty setting most casual players avoid and most committed players choose first. The brand names the audience by naming the setting.
Creative.manifesto: Most studios make games for the widest audience and round off the edges. Hard Mode makes games for the players who want the version with the edges intact. We design for the committed and assume the rest will find their way in.
Creative.industrySummary: Indie and mid-size game studios have been chasing accessibility. The opening at the other end is studios that lean into difficulty, depth, and demanding design. Players will buy them. They are already buying them.
Creative.competitorLandscape: FromSoftware (fromsoftware.jp) holds the cultural peak of difficulty-as-brand. ZA/UM (zaumstudio.com) before its troubles, did the literary difficult game. Cardboard Computer (cardboardcomputer.com) does the slow demanding side. We sit in their company, with a sharper visual brand.
Creative.positioningStatement: A studio that makes games for players who like the harder option.

targetAudience.primary: Players in their 20s and 30s who have completed at least one FromSoftware game. They wear the merch. They quote the boss fights. They tell other players they should try it.

dos: Be honest about how hard the game is
Quote real player frustrations in marketing
donts: Lower the floor of the experience

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark in a heavy display sans, with the M of MODE stylized as a small swordpoint or barbed edge. Standalone barbed-M icon for stickers, hoodies, and Steam profiles. The mark works on a charcoal background and nowhere else.

typography.secondary: PP Neue Montreal for body and product UI

customSections.title: What it isn't
customSections.body: Not for casual players first. Not for the accessibility-marketing crowd. Not afraid of red. Not too cool to put the boss quote on a tee.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: Hoodies that quote the worst boss line. Stickers shipped with every physical edition. A Discord server for the players who finished the games. Limited physical editions with art books that don't explain the lore.
